Community Aspirations
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Heritage & Environment, the following are the community aspirations:
Heritage & Tourism

The parish is home to a wealth of heritage assets, and the historic environment has been identified through public consultation as being of particular importance to local residents. Specifically, it is a community aspiration to ensure that the heritage is adequately protected and supported. Events and assets such as the rural museum and Ramsey 1940s Camp are important both to the heritage of the area and the tourism offer.
Potential linkages to proposed major tourism provision at Bedford should be considered to see how the wider sub region can benefit from tourism investment and visitors.

In order to protect the heritage of the area, protection of areas like Stocking Fen and the area north  of  Tesco should  be  secured. Retaining  Ramsey  and  Bury  as distinct  settlements  is fundamental to the history of Ramsey; so, protecting a gap between Bury and Ramsey through maintaining a settlement break is a significant community aspiration.
The agricultural origins of the parish are a fundamental part of the character of the area. The preservation of agriculture and the agricultural heritage and culture is therefore important.
Great Fen & Biodiversity
The Great Fen project extends into Ramsey Heights and Ramsey St Mary’s, linkages to the Great Fen waterways plan and visitor centre is important.

The  biodiversity of  the  area and the protection  of  green  spaces is  important  to  allow  the communities  to enjoy  the  outside  for  recreation  and  views;  whilst  limiting  recreational disturbance to Woodwalton Fen which is a designated nature conservation site.
Protecting  and  enhancing  the rights  of  ways  and  paths would  contribute  to  the  health  and enjoyment of the local community.
The implications of flood risk should be considered in all aspects of life and development.

24. Natural Environment

24.1 Most  of  the parish  of Ramsey is rural  and contains  substantial  areas  of  farmland  which contributes  significantly  to  the  character  of  the parish  and  the  setting  of  the town  and villages.

24.2 There is a need to assess the likelihood of proposals or policies within a Neighbourhood Plan having a significant effect on the ‘National Sites Network’ consisting of areas designated as Special Areas of Conservation (SAC) or Special Protection Areas (SPA’s). Consideration of the internationally designated Ramsar sites is also necessary; many Ramsar sites are also SACs or  SPAs. In  the  vicinity  of the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area  the ‘National Sites Network’ of interest  are  the Orton  Pit  SAC  (Peterborough); Nene  Washes  SPA/Ramsar (East  of Peterborough);   Ouse   Washes   SAC/SPA/Ramsar (North-west   of   Ely);   Portholme   SAC (Huntingdon/Godmanchester); and Fenland SAC/Woodwalton Fen Ramsar.
24.3 The  closest  to  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area is  the Fenland  SAC/Woodwalton  Fen  Ramsar which immediately abuts the south-west corner of the parish near Ramsey Heights.

24.4 SACs  were  previously  classified  in  accordance  with  EC  Directive  92/43/EEC  on  the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora (the Habitats Directive). Article 3  of  this  Directive  requires  the  establishment  of  a  European  network  of  important high‐ quality  conservation  sites  that  will  make  a  significant  contribution  to  conserving  the  189 habitat types and 788 species identified in Annexes I and II of the Directive. These sites are now  designated  under  the  Conservation  of  Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  (as amended).

24.5 SPAs  were  sites  first  classified  in  accordance  with  Article  4  of  the  EC  Directive  on  the conservation of wild birds (79/409/EEC), more commonly known as the Birds Directive. They were classified for rare and vulnerable birds, listed in Annex I to the Birds Directive, and for regularly occurring migratory species. These SPA sites are now designated under the Wildlife
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)
60 &  Countryside  Act  1981  (as  amended)  and  the  Conservation  (Natural  Habitats,  &  c.) Regulations 2010 (as amended).

24.6 Ramsar Sites are designated under the International Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat (the Ramsar Convention, Iran 1971 and amended by  the  Paris  Protocol  1992).  Although Ramsar  Sites are not protected in law by domestic  UK  legislation  as  a  matter  of policy   government, has   decreed   that unless   otherwise   specified   procedures relating  to  SPAs  and  SACs  will  also  apply to Ramsar Sites.

24.7 The    Habitats    Regulation    Assessment screening identifies that the Neighbourhood  Plan  proposals  would  not individually  or  cumulatively  result  in  any potential    significant    effects    on    any designated site.

24.8 The plan area contains no National Nature Reserves (NNR), Woodwalton Fen is also a NNR in addition to being a SAC and Ramsar  site. The other nearest NNR are at Upwood Meadows around 2km to the south-west and Holme Fen around 2km to the west of Ramsey St Mary’s. The Plan area contains no Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs). Woodwalton Fen is also a SSSI in addition to being an NNR, SAC and Ramsar site; Holme Fen is also a SSSI as well as being an NNR. Warboys  and  Wistow  Woods  SSSI  lies around  3km  to  the  south  of  Ramsey (town).

24.9 There are impact zones defined around the various designated sites to identify what scale of different types of development need consultation with Natural England. This principally impacts  on  Ramsey  Heights  and  Ramsey  St  Mary’s,  although  the  impact  zones  do  extend further across the Parish. These impact zones are shown in Appendix 1.

24.10 In  terms  of County  level  locally  designated  sites (County  Wildlife  Sites),  the  plan  area contains Ramsey Heights Nature Reserve and Reservoir East of Park Farm which lies north- east of Ramsey towards Ramsey Hollow.

24.11 The Great Fen Project Area extends into the western part of the parish near Ramsey Heights and Ramsey St Mary’s. The Great Fen Landscape & Visual Setting boundary extends across the western part of the parish, covering land west of Ugg Mere Court Road in Ramsey Heights and west of the B1040 in Ramsey St Mary’s.

24.12 The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS 44 ) is a bold new plan to revive and protect nature across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. It’s a locally driven, government-backed initiative that maps out where and how we can restore habitats, boost biodiversity, and reconnect people with the natural world, from countryside to city parks.

Parts of Ramsey lie within Flood Zone 3, this extends across the northern part of  the  town  including  Stocking  Fen  Road,  The  Moorings,  Kingfisher  Way,  Mallard  Close, Millfields,  Turvers  Lane  and  parts  of  Mill  Lane.  Recent  areas  along  the  western  edge  of Ramsey  that  have  been  developed  north  and  south  of  Biggin  Lane  contain  a  watercourse route that also lies within Flood Zone 3. The Ramsey Golf Course area including the southern side of Hollow Lane is also within Flood Zone 3. There has been significant flooding in the past.

26.2 Surface  water  flooding  potential  affects  much  of  the  parish  of  Ramsey.  Surface  water flooding  is  a  matter  to  be  taken  into  account  in  the  planning  application  process 49 . The Neighbourhood Plan alongside the Local Plan and the NPPF strives to promote sustainable drainage techniques (SuDS).

26.3 Fluvial (river) flooding and surface water flooding risks change over  time, in part at least due to the impact of climate change. Developers when designing surface water systems have to design them with an allowance for climate change 50 . During December 2020 there were a large volume of flood incidents across Cambridgeshire, Ramsey was affected. The Lead Local Flood Authority (LLFA) undertook a statutory flood investigation and produced the relevant report 51 .

26.4 SuDS   are   an   approach   to   managing surface  water  run-off  which  seeks  to mimic  natural  drainage  systems  and retain  water  on  or  near  the  site  as opposed     to     traditional     drainage approaches which involve piping water off  site  as  quickly  as  possible.  SuDS offer    significant    advantages    over conventional piped drainage systems in reducing  flood  risk  by  attenuating  the rate and quantity of surface water run- off from a site, promoting groundwater recharge, and improving water quality, biodiversity and amenity. The LLFA would particularly support above-ground open SuDS such as wetlands, attenuation basins, ponds and swales as they provide additional amenity and biodiversity benefits.

26.5 Opportunities for increasing biodiversity at opportunity sites and in the protected settlement breaks are  discussed  within  the  Neighbourhood  Plan. There  is  a potential  for  increasing biodiversity through the use of SuDS features such as attenuation basins, ponds and swales in these circumstances.

The area is one of the important open areas in this part of the town that forms part of the overall significance of the Conservation Area. The field has a parkland character from the mature trees within it.

The Conservation Area Character Appraisal identifies that the Cemetery and Rural Museum form a buffer between the housing area of the town and this open land. The verdant and undeveloped nature  of  the  area  contributes  strongly  to  the  character  and  appearance  of  this  part  of  the Conservation Area.

The  land  is  abutted  on  both  sides  by  the Ramsey Rural Museum and the Ramsey 1940s Camp. It  has  historical  significance  through helping  both  of  those  attractions  tell  the story of the history of the town through the various events hosted on the land.

This  space  is  an  integral  part  of  Ramsey’s heritage.  Currently, the field is used for the maximum allowable events throughout the year. It links the Rural Museum and the Ramsey 1940s Camp  and  allows  for  highly  successful  joint  ventures  as  well  as  solo  events.  Without  it,  large community and nationally recognised events will no longer be able to occur causing loss of funding for both the Ramsey 1940s Camp and Ramsey Rural Museum. This could jeopardise the viability of both sites.

Historically, the side of the Museum protruding into the field was identified as an historic track and is adjacent to  what  is  believed  to  be  the  boundary  of  the  Abbey precinct 53 . There is also a possibility of ordinance from the Ramsey 1940s Camp from when it was a searchlight facility during World War II.  The area of the Camp was used during World War I, but documentation associated with  that  appears  to  be  sealed,  possibly  under  the Official Secrets Act.

The area is effectively an events space and showground where  a  significant  number  of  public  events  are  held. These  events  are  integral  to  the  cultural,  social  and  economic  life  of  the  community,  local businesses and attractions. Events held include the 1940s Weekend, the Fen Fair, Country Fair and Plough Day, Ramsey Steam & Fire Show. These events can have up to 3,500 people attending. The  area  of  Ramsey  Town  Moorings  on  the  High  Lode  has  been  partially  altered  through  the development The Moorings off Stocking Fen Road. It is at the point where High  Lode  changes  from  being  an  open-air waterway   to   becoming   an   underground waterway   running   southwards   under  The Great  Whyte  through  the  Ramsey  Tunnels after going through the Mill Sluice.

In around 2022 some 120m of new permanent visitor  moorings  were  completed  on  the eastern  side.  These  visitor  moorings  are owned  and  maintained  by  the  Middle  Level Commissioners   and   were   made   possible following  the  change  in  focus  and  funding arising  from  the  2018  Middle  Level  Act  and the introduction of licensing. The land beyond the bank has recently transferred from the housing developer to Ramsey Town Council.

It  has  historic  significance  as  the  waterway  adjacent  to  the  Corn  Mill  now  known  as  Rivermill Apartments and as part of the nineteenth century industrial area. That character area within the Ramsey  Conservation  Area  contained  the  LNER  Holme  &  Ramsey  Branch  line  which  hosted  the North  Station,  where  North  Station  Close  is  currently  sited.  The  importance  of  the  Ramsey northern gateway goes back to Saxon times, which is the most likely time that the navigable Lodes became the chief form of commercial transport for the town.

The  waterway  has  a  natural  beauty  although  further  enhancement  of  the  public  realm  would improve the overall beauty of this gateway. The eastern side of the moorings has a modern quay; the  western  side  of  the  moorings has an older quayside. The moorings support  recreational  use  of  High Lode  as  a  navigable  waterway  and provides   a   modern   recreational gateway into the town which could be developed further.

The waterway and its banks provide an    important    contribution    to wildlife  richness,  in  an  area  which has over time become quite densely developed.    Notwithstanding    the nature of the B1040 passing by the moorings, the area still provides an opportunity for tranquillity.

82 Theme – Infrastructure
Community Aspirations
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Infrastructure, the following are the community aspirations:
Transport & Parking
The road network across the villages is in a poor  physical condition and a solution to the roads being susceptible and badly impacted by ground movement needs to be explored.

The villages have a lack of footways; in the town the footways are narrow and are a challenge to navigate at certain times, such as on bin day. As the number of bins increases there needs to be exploration into different  solutions, solar  compacting  bins  for  example that  might  assist  in mitigating the size and number of bins on the footway.

Ramsey town has high levels of on-street parking, and the town centre struggles with not having sufficient parking provision to meet the needs of shoppers and those who live and work within the town  centre. Opportunities  to  secure  additional  provision  and  access  to  cost-effective  public electric vehicle charging also need to be explored.
Accessibility/Connectivity

Connectivity between the villages is poor, as is connectivity between the villages and the town. The  geographic  isolation  of  the  parish  means  that  the  provision  of  good  phone  and  internet connection  /  signal/  coverage is  vital. Local  support  for  the services  in  town – dentists, GP’s, district nurses, physios etc. needs to occur. This can include support for these services to diversify their  health  offer  and provide  the  opportunity  for  outreach  hospital services  where  feasible. Hospital facilities are difficult to get to if you do not drive.

Balanced development is wanted to support a thriving community of all ages. Including support for family members to stay in the area throughout their lives; thereby keeping and supporting the local  connection which  is  a  vital  component  of  the  community  spirit  which  was  evident  in  the public consultation responses. Employment opportunities with small start-ups and industrial units as well as shops is important.

Ensuring  that  we  signpost  services  for  those  with  disabilities,  children  and  the  elderly is  an important aspiration. An aging community needs support for aspects like the community bus/ cars to provide connection to the larger towns and cities.

We recognise that the villages around Ramsey are growing and are bringing more traffic, shoppers and people wanting to access services in the town. Due to the poor accessibility and connectivity, new development results in use of the private car rather than active travel modes such as walking and cycling. It is a community aspiration to maintain the culture, the things that make the villages and town unique  and  the  community  feel.  Overall  rural  tourism  is  preferrable  and  more appropriate than housing to maintain that culture.

29.1 The Huntingdonshire   Developer   Contributions SPD 55 sets   out   the   need   to   secure infrastructure and developer contributions from new development in the form of: • Affordable Housing • Green Space • Footpaths and Access • Health • Community Facilities • Libraries and Lifelong Learning • Education and Schools • Residential Wheeled Bins (Note - The costs are updated regularly the 2023/2024 updated costs can be found on the Huntingdonshire website 56 )

29.2 Policy LP  4 - Contributing  to  Infrastructure  Delivery in  the  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to 2036 sets  out  the focus  at  the district level to  secure  infrastructure  and  developer contributions from new development in the form of: • Affordable housing • Recreation (including leisure and sports facilities) • Green infrastructure and biodiversity enhancement/mitigation • Transport • Community facilities • Education, health and social care and community safety • Utilities infrastructure and energy • Emergency and essential services • Environmental improvements • Drainage and flood prevention and protection • Waste recycling facilities • Public art, heritage and archaeology

29.3 The Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) 57 allows local planning authorities to raise funds from  new  development.  The  money  raised  is  used  to  fund  district-wide  and  local infrastructure    projects    that benefit local communities. The CIL charges  are  based  on  the size and type of development. For most developments the CIL charges  are  designed  to  cater for  the required infrastructure provision. For large scale major development 58 there  is  still  a need for infrastructure provision  that  will  not  be  CIL funded.  Therefore section  106 planning  obligations will  still be used as appropriate. The CIL Charging  Schedule 59 has  to  be kept under review with regard to viability considerations so may change during the lifetime of this Neighbourhood Plan.

29.7 Huntingdonshire  District  Council  and the  Cambridgeshire  and Peterborough Combined   Authority   produced   the Ramsey    Prospectus    for Growth 60 . 29.8 Improvements to local infrastructure are underway. 30.1 Local planning policy recognises that Ramsey and the surrounding area has relatively poor transport infrastructure, being well off the primary road network and relatively remote. Its comparatively  limited  services,  facilities  and  employment  opportunities  make  it  a  less sustainable   location   in   terms  of   travel   than   some  of   the  other   market   towns   in Cambridgeshire.

30.2 Ramsey and the surrounding villages are classed as a rural area, there are high levels of car ownership  and  reliance  on  the  car  to  maintain  access  to  key  services. Some  87.7%  of households  in  the  parish  of  Ramsey have  one or  more  cars/vans,  with almost  half  of  the households having two, three or more cars/vans. In addition, high house prices and lack of affordable housing has led to more people travelling further to work, with the average length of commute in Ramsey greater than the national average. Access to employment, education and services can be a real challenge without a car in rural areas.

30.3 The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to 2036  contains  Policy  LP  16  which indicates that new development will be  expected  to  contribute  to  an enhanced  transport  network  that supports an increasing proportion of journeys    being    undertaken    by sustainable travel modes.

30.4 Access    to    high    quality    public transport  is  known  to  be  hugely beneficial  to  improving  access  to services for  those members of society who cannot,  for a variety of reasons, access a car. This is particularly acute in rural areas such as Ramsey where distances between households and essential services are often large, making walking and cycling less practical than in urban areas. The villages in the parish are reliant upon Ramsey town for many higher order services and facilities. However, the town doesn’t provide all essential services and journeys to larger settlements  such  as  Peterborough or  Huntingdon  are  necessary,  for  example to  access hospital services, higher education and many public services. The Town Council alongside the  Ramsey  Neighbourhood Trust 64 does  look  to  support  the  provision  of  outreach public services to improve accessibility.

30.5 It  has  recently  been  announced  that  there  will  be  a  new  direct  bus  service (X31) from Upwood, Bury and Ramsey to Peterborough from January 2026. This will be operated under the new Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority contract 65 .

30.6 The geographic nature of the parish makes it difficult for residents of the villages to access the services and facilities in Ramsey town centre by walking and cycling. The distances in combination with the lack of footways and uneven road surfaces due to the fenland geology are barriers to walking and cycling.

30.7 The Vision for Ramsey document (extract overleaf) sets out a number of transport initiatives that the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority and Huntingdonshire District Council have developed.

30.8 The  Government  through  Active  Travel  England is  looking  to  make  walking,  wheeling  and cycling the preferred choice for everyone to get around in England. Active travel is the term often  used  to encompass  elements  such  as  walking  to  school,  cycling  to  work,  or  other everyday journeys you make to get from place to place, rather than just walking or cycling solely for leisure or fitness. In addition, active travel can offer a convenient, accessible and affordable way to move more for shorter journeys. National policy in the NPPF does not refer to active travel but instead refers to sustainable transport but includes that policies should look for opportunities to promote walking, cycling and public transport use are identified and  pursued.  Active  travel  and sustainable  travel  modes not  only  positively  contribute  to addressing climate change but also can assist in maintaining a healthy community.

31. Highway Impact

31.1 The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036  contains Policy  LP  16  on  Sustainable  Travel  and Policy  LP  17 on Parking Provision  and  Vehicle Movement.  This latter policy  indicates  that
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)
90 proposals  must incorporate  adequate  parking  for  vehicles  and  cycles.  Advice  on  parking arrangements is contained in the Huntingdonshire Design Guide SPD (2017) 71 .

30.2 Early consultation identified a significant level of concern regarding the volume of traffic and road safety. There was also a significant level of concern about the road infrastructure and  difficulties  with parking.  Improving  road safety  would  enhance  the  quality of life of some of the most vulnerable members of the community. Unfortunately, traffic management is not an issue over which the Town Council has direct control. Most of the traffic originates outside the parish. As a consequence, traffic management cannot be easily addressed by this Neighbourhood  Plan.  However,  the Town  Council will  seek  to  support road  safety improvements around the plan area.

30.3 As part of the overall approach, the Neighbourhood Plan can support and ensure that new development  does  not  adversely  affect  the  highway  network; or  that  where  it  does, contributions through    a    Planning Obligation address     the     impacts appropriately. However, a Planning Obligation can only be sought where it meets the relevant tests; namely: it is necessary  to  make  the  development acceptable   in   planning   terms;   is directly  related  to  the  development; and is fairly and reasonably related in scale   and   kind. In   some cases, Cambridgeshire   County   Council   is seeking  more  direct  off-site  delivery of highway improvements, i.e. rather than paying the County Council a fee the  developer  will  undertake  the  works  in  the highway  directly. As such  in  some  cases  a planning  condition  may  be  the  appropriate  implementation  measure.  In  some cases, Community Infrastructure Levy monies will cover highway improvements.

30.4 The  policy  includes  reference  to the  storage  and  collection  of  refuse  bins as  where insufficient on-site provision is made this can result in a highway impact. This impact involves bins blocking pedestrian use of footways that can lead to pedestrian and vehicle conflict. The Cambridgeshire RECAP Waste Management Design Guide SPD 72 sets out advice on access, maximum travel distances, number of bins per property type etc. and takes into account the Council’s  Waste  Collection  Policies. The  policy looks  to provide  the  opportunity  for developers to promote alternative or innovative methods of storage such as underground bin storage,  for  example on larger sites if viability and operational practicalities support this approach  in  a development. Alternative  or  innovative  methods of storage could have the added benefit of improving the visual aspects of recycling and waste management for the benefit of the community, particularly where smaller dwellings are concentrated, and the provision of wheeled bins may be less desirable.

30.5 Where parking courts are proposed, care needs to be taken. These spaces often suffer from poor  natural surveillance, limited  overlooking  and  can  become  unsafe or underused.  It  is recommended in the policy that parking courts should only be used where they are small, well-overlooked,   incorporate   high   quality   and   subtle   use   of materials,   integrated landscaping and trees. The HDC Design Guide SPD 2017 on page 89 provides more detailed advice.

Policy 9 – Highway Impact

Proposals  will be supported  where they  would  not  adversely  affect  the  local  highway  network. Where proposals would negatively  impact  on  the local highway  network,  contributions  will  be sought, where appropriate, through a Planning Obligation to minimise and mitigate those impacts associated with the development.

Any new development which involves alterations to existing highways and the provision of new highways would be supported where it meets the following design criteria: • Provides suitable measures to accommodate traffic (including at peak times); • Improve the safety and attractiveness of the street scene; and • Integrate appropriate traffic-calming measures within the development.

Development  should  incorporate  adequate dedicated on-site  provision  for  parking within  the curtilage  of  properties  or  in small and  well-overlooked parking  courts  or  similar. Development proposals which would result in the displacement of existing off-street parking provision to on- street parking will not be supported. Proposals that incorporate car-free areas such as play streets would be supported.

New development should incorporate adequate on-site provision for the storage and collection of refuse  bins. Where  appropriate  refuse  collection  storage  should  be  screened  and be easily accessible to the collection point. Where developers want to promote alternative or innovative methods of storage such as underground bin storage where viability and operational practicalities allow this would be supported; particularly where this improves the visual aspects of recycling and waste management for the benefit of the community.
32. Rights of Way Network

32.1 Ramsey covers a large area of countryside and as a consequence it would be expected that it may benefit from an extensive and well-used rights of way network. However, across the parish as a whole there are relatively limited public rights of way. It is possible to get from Ramsey Forty Foot and Ramsey Heights  to Ramsey.  Ramsey St Mary’s by contrast  has  no public rights of way.

32.2 An effective rights of way network provides a dual role for recreation and for sustainable travel. Their recreational use makes an important contribution to health and well-being. The  areas  allocated  for  housing  are  distant  from  the  main services  and  facilities  in Ramsey. As  such  the right of  way network  contributes  to  accessibility  and  providing  the opportunity for sustainable travel using non-vehicle modes. The  Neighbourhood  Plan  looks  to  improve  and  extend  the rights of way network.

32.3 Current provision for pedestrians and cyclists is not significant. Consultation identified the lack of  connection  between  the  villages  and  town  to be  an  issue. There  are  a  number  of footpaths and footways that pass through the town, including footways in the centre of the town that are narrow  and/or  are  in poor quality,  with  the  High  Street being  a  particular example. Narrow streets and on street parking also make cycling difficult and increase the feeling of danger, particularly for young people travelling to school.

Monitoring and Review

34.1 Continual plan review is a fundamental element of the planning system. It is important to check that the plan is being implemented correctly, ensure that outcomes match objectives and to change the plan if they are not.  This Neighbourhood Plan will be carefully monitored by  the Town Council and  reviewed  if  it  becomes  apparent  that  the vision,  goals and objectives of the Plan are not being met.

34.2 Monitoring  is  a  shared  responsibility  of  the Town Council  as  the  qualifying  body; Huntingdonshire  District  Council  as  the  Local  Planning  Authority;  and  users  of  the Neighbourhood Plan. The Town Council will consider the effectiveness of the policies and proposals  in  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  each  time  it  makes  representations  on  a  planning application;  alongside  seeking  views  on  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  at  each  Annual  Parish Meeting. The Town Council will request Huntingdonshire District Council to raise with it any issues  arising  out  of  the  development  management  process  in  determining  individual planning applications. Users of the Neighbourhood Plan are encouraged to make comments on monitoring of the Neighbourhood Plan to the Town Council at any point.

34.3 The Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared to guide development up to 2046. It is unlikely that the Neighbourhood Plan will remain current and entirely relevant for  the entire plan period and may, in whole or in part, require some amendments before 2046.

Local Plan: A plan for  the future development of a local area, drawn up by the local planning authority in consultation with the community. In law this is described as the development plan documents adopted under the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004. A local plan can consist of either strategic or non-strategic policies, or a combination of the two.

Neighbourhood  plans: A  plan  prepared  by  a  parish  council  or  neighbourhood  forum  for  a designated neighbourhood area. In law this is described as a neighbourhood development plan in the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004.

NPPF *: National Planning Policy Framework, this forms the overall planning policy produced by the Government to inform the making of Development Plans including Neighbourhood Plans and decision making on planning applications.

Open space: All open space of public value, including not just land, but also areas of water (such as rivers, canals, lakes and reservoirs) which offer important opportunities for sport and recreation and can act as a visual amenity.

Policies  Map *: A  document  which  illustrates  on  a  base  map  all  the  policies  and  proposals contained in this Neighbourhood Plan or another document which forms part of the Development Plan.

Planning condition: A condition imposed on a grant of planning permission (in accordance with the Town and Country Planning Act 1990) or a condition included in a Local Development Order or Neighbourhood Development Order.
Planning obligation: A legally enforceable obligation entered into under section 106 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to mitigate the impacts of a development proposal.

Planning  Practice  Guidance  *: this  forms  the  overall  national  planning  practice  guidance  and advice  produced  by  the  Government  to  inform  the  making  of  Development  Plans  including Neighbourhood Plans and decision making on planning applications.
Ramsar  sites:  Wetlands  of  international  importance,  designated  under  the  1971 Ramsar Convention.

Rural exception sites: Small sites used for affordable housing in perpetuity where sites would not normally be used for housing. Rural exception sites seek to address the needs of the local community by accommodating households who are either current residents or have an existing family or employment connection. A proportion of market homes may be allowed on the site at the local planning authority’s discretion, for example where essential to enable the delivery of affordable units without grant funding. [Also see Policy LP 28 of the Local Plan]
Scheduled Monument *: Those monuments that are given legal protection by being scheduled by Historic England.
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)

Self-build and custom-build housing:  Housing built by an individual,  a group of individuals, or persons working with or for them, to be occupied by that individual. Such housing can be either market or  affordable housing. A legal definition, for  the purpose of applying the Self-build and Custom Housebuilding Act 2015 (as amended), is contained in section 1(A1) and (A2) of that Act.

Setting of a heritage asset: The surroundings in which a heritage asset is experienced. Its extent is not fixed and may change as the asset and its surroundings evolve. Elements of a setting may make a positive or negative contribution to the significance of an asset, may affect the ability to appreciate that significance or may be neutral.

Settlement  Boundary *: The  boundary  drawn  around  various  towns  and  villages  to  limit  new development and define the ‘built-up area’ of the settlement. Outside of the settlement boundary is considered to be the countryside.

Significance (for heritage policy): The value of a heritage asset to this and future generations because  of  its  heritage  interest.  The  interest  may  be  archaeological,  architectural,  artistic  or historic. Significance derives not only from a heritage asset’s physical presence, but also from its setting.  For  World  Heritage  Sites,  the  cultural value described within each site’s Statement of Outstanding Universal Value forms part of its significance.

Special  Areas  of  Conservation  (SAC):  Areas  defined  by  regulation  3  of  the  Conservation  of Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  given  special  protection  as  important conservation sites.

Special  Protection  Areas  (SPA):  Areas  classified  under  regulation  15  of  the  Conservation  of Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  identified  as  being  of  international importance for the breeding, feeding, wintering or the migration of rare and vulnerable species of birds.
Site  of  Special Scientific  Interest:  Sites designated  by  Natural  England  under  the  Wildlife  and Countryside Act 1981.

Strategic Environmental Assessment: A procedure (set out in the Environmental Assessment of Plans and Programmes Regulations 2004) which requires the formal environmental assessment of certain plans and programmes which are likely to have significant effects on the environment.

Supplementary planning documents: Documents which add further detail to the policies in the Local Plan. They can be used to provide further guidance for development on specific sites, or on particular  issues,  such  as  design.  Supplementary  planning  documents  are  capable  of  being  a material consideration in planning decisions but are not part of the development plan.

Sustainable transport modes: Any efficient, safe and accessible means of transport with overall low  impact  on  the  environment,  including  walking  and  cycling,  low  and  ultra-low  emission vehicles, car sharing and public transport.
Windfall sites: Sites not specifically identified in the development plan.

metadata.title: Robert Pattinson announced as the next actor to play James Bond
metadata.contentSnippet: Robert Pattinson has been officially announced as the next actor to play James Bond after a lengthy casting process

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Robert Pattinson announced as the next actor to play James Bond
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next actor to play James Bond. The 40-year-old was revealed in a series of Instagram posts on the official franchise account. It comes after a lengthy casting process in which several names were rumoured to be in the running for the role. This included the likes of Slow Horses star Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor and Nicholas Hoult. Pattinson succeeds Daniel Craig in the role, who last played the character in 2021's No Time to Die. In a statement reported by Variety, Pattinson said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime. "I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. "To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. "I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team." Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next James Bond film and discussed Pattinson's casting. He shared: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. "He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin." Robert Pattinson is an English actor who began appearing in TV and film roles in 2004. He is best known for playing Edward Cullen in The Twilight Saga films, Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire and Bruce Wayne/Batman in 2022's The Batman. Other major films he has appeared in include Tenet, Mickey 17, The Lighthouse and Die My Love. In 2026, Pattinson has featured in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, The Drama and Primetime, and he will also appear in Dune: Part Three as Scytale. How do you feel about Robert Pattinson being cast as the next James Bond? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: Ready Steady Roll: award-winning café offers screen-free fun from £2
metadata.contentSnippet: Ready Steady Roll review: discover the welcoming Sharnbrook board game café near Kimbolton, with hundreds of games, food, drinks and sessions for all ages.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Ready Steady Roll: award-winning café offers screen-free fun from £2
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Kath Sansom recently visited Ready Steady Roll, which has two sites - one near Kimbolton, and another in Peterborough - here's what she thought In an age when so much socialising revolves around screens, there's something really refreshing about gathering around a table, picking up some board games and spending a few hours laughing with friends. Ready Steady Roll is the sort of place you could easily drive past without ever knowing it exists. Yet this award-winning board game café was exactly what we were looking for when we stumbled on it during a Google search while looking for a halfway meeting place that offered more than the usual coffee shop or pub catch-up. As life gets busier, maintaining friendships when living in different towns many miles apart can become surprisingly difficult – so finding somewhere worth travelling to is a challenge. Thankfully, Ready Steady Roll offered the perfect solution, with an afternoon packed with laughter, nostalgia and friendly competition. The venue boasts an extensive games library with options ranging from light-hearted family favourites to deeper strategy games. Our afternoon began in unfamiliar territory with Shoot for the Stars, a “general knowledge” game with questions like how many beans in a can of Heinz. We then opted for a healthy dose of nostalgia, transporting back to childhood with the classics Frustration and Operation, before picking up Doodle Rush, a quick-fire drawing game. Whether you're a seasoned gamer or someone whose experience begins and ends with Ludo and Monopoly, there's something to tempt everyone of all ages with every genre imaginable neatly packed on well organised shelves – most of which we'd never heard of before. Board games are only half the story. The café serves a great selection of food and drinks, and we happily worked our way through impressive coffee, chips, sausage rolls and cakes during our four-hour visit. The table service meant we could stay immersed in the games while the food and drinks arrived at our table, helping create an unhurried atmosphere. Perhaps what stood out most was the welcome. The venue feels warm, cosy and genuinely inviting, somewhere that encourages you to settle in and stay awhile. It was a joy to escape to. There is also a strong community feel. Alongside regular daytime gaming, the venue hosts board-game evenings where people can come along, meet fellow enthusiasts and join games with others. For anyone looking to expand their social circle or simply find opponents for a favourite game, it's a lovely idea. What makes Ready Steady Roll special is that it offers something increasingly rare: a chance to slow down. No notifications, no scrolling, no rush. Just good company, good food, plenty of laughter and hundreds of games waiting to be explored. For three friends from across the region, Ready Steady Roll turned an ordinary catch-up into a memorable day out, leaving us already planning our next visit. Need to Know Where: Studio 5, Ivy Lodge, Rushden Road, Sharnbrook, MK44 1ND. Cost: £4 for adults and £3 for children for a two-hour session. Weekday term-time sessions are £2. Opening times: check the Ready Steady Roll website and social media channels for current opening hours.

metadata.title: Council 'does not intend to progress' plans to build on Hunts car parks
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdonshire District Council "does not intend to progress" Capital & Centric plans to build on car parks in St Neots, St Ives and Huntingdon.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Council 'does not intend to progress' plans to build on Hunts car parks
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. The council "does not intend to progress" plans to build housing developments on three Huntingdonshire car parks after 90% of residents opposed the scheme. Plans by developer Capital & Centric and Huntingdonshire District Council (HDC) to build homes on three large car parks in St Neots, Huntingdon and St Ives sparked fury among residents in August. The plans for the St Neots Tebbutts Road car park include two five-storey buildings, up to 83 homes and units for independent businesses. The newly released Gateway 1 report reveals that out of resident responses, 91.2% opposed the plans in St Ives, 89.8% opposed the plans in St Neots and 87% opposed the plans in Huntingdon. After the completion of the Gateway 1 stage, which included public engagement, technical surveys, and concept designs, the council "does not intend to progress to Gateway 2 with Capital and Centric on the current schemes", the report reveals. Residents turned out in force to share their views about the plans to develop Tebbutts Road (Image: Emily Stevens) In a statement, the council said: "The scale and consistency of public opposition is focused on the fundamental choice of sites rather than design detail; unresolved strategic parking and accessibility issues remain; and the economic case does not outweigh the identified concern regarding parking function and public feedback." The main concern raised was the impact of redeveloping central surface car parks on the vitality and accessibility of town centres. The council’s decision follows pre-application advice from the planning authority, which stressed the need for a comprehensive parking strategy before any redevelopment could be considered. Officers concluded that the evidence did not provide a strong enough case to justify further investment in the next stage of the project. An independent review of the Capital & Centric commission will continue, and the technical work completed to date will remain available for future use. The full report will be discussed at an extraordinary meeting of HDC at 7pm on Tuesday, November 24.

metadata.title: Councillors vote to approve 600-home plan for St Neots
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdonshire District Councillors have voted to approve a a plan for up to 600 new homes on land at Priory Hill in St Neots.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Councillors vote to approve 600-home plan for St Neots
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Councillors have voted to approve a a plan for up to 600 new homes in St Neots. The outline application by Bloor Homes for land at Priory Hill, north of St Neots would create a new neighbourhood between Priory Hill Road, Huntingdon Road, the River Great Ouse, and the East Coast Main Line. The site sits close to Priory Park (Image: Newsquest) St Neots Town Council and Little Paxton Parish Council have both lodged objections to the scheme. The town council said it is concerned that "the development would place additional pressure on local services and infrastructure, particularly secondary school provision" and raised additional concerns over loss of agricultural land, flood risk and drainage. Additionally, HDC has received a total of 92 objections from residents. At a meeting of Huntingdonshire District Council's Development Management Committee on November 16, councillors voted to approve the application in line with planning officer recommendations. Councillors debated the plan for more than two hours, initially rejecting the motion to approve the plan. After more debate, a motion to refuse the plans was proposed by Cllr Alan Hunt and seconded by Cllr Stephen Ferguson. The result was a tie of six votes for and six against, so Chair Cllr Warren Smith had the casting vote and rejected the motion to refuse. Cllr Tom Sanderson put forward a proposal to approve the application, which resulted in another tie of five votes for, five against and two abstentions. Cllr Warren Smith again had the casting vote and the motion to approve the plans was passed. The scheme seeks permission for up to 600 homes, with 40 per cent designated as affordable housing. Alongside the housing, the plans include a community hub, mobility hub, public open space, allotments, walking and cycling routes, landscaping, and associated infrastructure. There would also be changes to nearby road speed limits and junctions, along with the removal of a double-mini roundabout at Priory Hill.

metadata.title: National Grid statement over UK power outage rumours for November 19
metadata.contentSnippet: National Grid statement over UK power outage rumours for November 19, following claims circulating on social media.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: National Grid statement over UK power outage rumours for November 19
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: National Grid has reassured households that there is no national power outage expected on Thursday, November 19, following claims circulating on social media. The organisation issued a statement after becoming aware of a post claiming there would be a National Grid outage on the date. National Grid said: “We’re aware of a false social media post claiming there will be a National Grid outage on Thursday, November 19 2026. “There is no outage expected. Please disregard the post and report misinformation to social media platforms. “Check our official channels for accurate information.” The warning comes amid a number of unrelated rumours about major blackouts circulating online during November. Other claims suggesting a widespread blackout would take place on November 17 have also circulated internationally, with fact-checking reports finding no evidence of a planned worldwide power cut. The November 19 claim also coincides with the highly anticipated release date of Grand Theft Auto VI, although there is no verified evidence establishing that the game is the source of the outage rumour. National Grid is encouraging people who encounter the false claim to report it to the relevant social media platform and rely on its official channels for accurate information.

metadata.title: Former timber mill to be demolished for homes despite flooding and traffic fears
metadata.contentSnippet: A former saw mill on Histon Road in Cottenham will be demolished to make way for affordable homes despite fears from residents over increased traffic.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Former timber mill to be demolished for homes despite flooding and traffic fears
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A former village saw mill will be demolished to make way for affordable homes despite fears from residents over increased traffic. South Cambridgeshire District Council’s planning committee approved the proposal for 34 affordable homes at the former timber mill on Histon Road in Cottenham. Though the site lies on the green belt, planning officers recommended the scheme for approval as it was “proportionate to Cottenham village”. Luke Webb, planning director at the applicant Living Space Housing, said it would be a “positive use of a current brownfield site” and they aimed to start building as “early as possible in 2027”. Cottenham Parish Council objected to the plans as they feared they would overwhelm local infrastructure, noting that 34 homes had already been approved nearby. Jo Brook said the parish council recognises the need for affordable housing but this “does not automatically make every site suitable for development.”. She said families would face a half hour walk to primary school or nursery which would encourage them to drive. She said: “For families, that’s a considerable journey and many will inevitably choose to drive. “This is particularly concerning when the school is already exploring a scheme to close Lambs Lane at drop-off and collection times because of existing parking and congestion problems.” Ms Brook added that it is “well documented” that the surrounding properties on Histon Road “flood regularly”. Cllr Heather Williams, of The Mordens, said she “can completely understand” their concerns about the cumulative impact, but it has to be weighed against housing need. The Conservative councillor said: “We can see from the officer’s report that there is need and, to be quite frank, there is going to be an increasing need for a long time. “I think there is a danger with all these applications that you don’t end up actually putting all the social housing together and I would say that this is probably its limit for that.” Cllr Dr Martin Cahn, of Histon and Impington, said that Cottenham is “a very unusual village” as it is “an extremely long village”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “Where is the centre? It’s strung along a long distance – any development in Cottenham is going to be too far from some of the facilities. “I don’t see that as a reason to refuse it and it will be a valuable addition to our social housing, which is a high priority in our district.” Cllr Anna Bradnam, chair of the committee, said there was a “substantial justification” for housing in the area and added that the proposal now has a “very comprehensive surface water drainage scheme”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “It’s possible that this will actually make it less likely that those properties on Histon Road flood – let us hope so.” The plans were approved unanimously by the planning committee.

MINUTES OF RAMSEY TOWN COUNCIL MEETING 
held at 7pm on Thursday 27 August 2026 at  
Ramsey Town Council Great Whyte, Ramsey 
 
 
Present:  Councillors: I Axelsen, J Bufton, J Clarke, M Clarke, V Fendley (Mayor), S Fice, R 
Terrill, J Thompson, and  L Webster. 
In attendance: Mrs A Jerrom, Deputy Town Clerk  
 
The Chairman welcomed new Councillor Jessie Thompson to the meeting. 
 
289. Apologies for Absence. 
Cllrs J Aubin, A Austin, S Corney, A Costello, L Knight, C Maskell and P Rose. 
 
290.To Receive Declarations of Interest. 
No declarations of interest were made. 
 
291. Public Participation. 
There were no members of the public present. 
 
292. Minutes of the Last Meeting to be Approved. 
Councillors  voted with  two  abstentions to  accept  the Minutes  of the meeting  of the  Council 
held on 13
th
 August 2026 as a correct record. 
 
293. Planning Applications for Consideration. 
1.1 26/01416/HHFUL – Two  storey extension,  barn and  carport,  internal  and  external 
alterations,  new  dormer and  canopy  roofs  and  installation  of  solar  PV  panels – Heathfield, 
Benwick Road, Ramsey Forty Foot  Proposed by Cllr S Fice and seconded by Cllr L Webster 
Ramsey Town Council voted unanimously for Huntingdonshire District Council to APPROVE 
the application as per their decision on a previous application for the property in June 2026, 
which had since been withdrawn. 
1.2  26/01206/OUT – Proposed  demolition  of  an  existing  dwelling  and  outbuilding  and 
replacement  with  4  new  dwellings  (outline  application with  all  matters  reserved,  with  the 
exception of access) – 190 Herne Road, Ramsey St Marys.  Having been proposed by Cllr J 
Clarke and seconded by Cllr Terrill, councillors voted unanimously to recommend refusal of the 
application  due  to  the  lack  of information  regarding adequate parking,  particularly  for  the 
bungalows  at  the  rear  of  the  development.    They  also had  concerns  regarding  the  possible 
precedent that might be set for development at the rear of properties in the village. 
1.3 26/01484/TREE – G1  (dead  Silver  Birch) – fell  and remove – Cedar  Lodge,  St Marys 
Road,  Ramsey. Having  been  proposed  by  Cllr  S  Fice  and  seconded  by  Cllr  L  Webster 
councillors voted unanimously to make no observations either in favour or against the proposal 
but to leave the decision to the arboricultural officer. 
 
294.  Consultation on the Reviewed Bury Draft Neighbourhood Plan. 
Councillors discussed the suggested response to the consultation previously circulated by 
Cllr Fendley. It was agreed that there would be infrastructure implications for Ramsey 
following the growth within the Bury Neighbourhood Plan area. It was therefore proposed by 
Cllr Bufton, seconded by Cllr Terrill and agreed with one abstention to submit that response 
from the Town Council which included the acknowledgment of the need for Infrastructure 
Levy(CIL) contributions towards car parking provision at Mews Close and electric charging 
points which would serve the wider community. 
 
 
 

2 
 
295. Update on Emergency Response – Holme Fen. 
Councillor Fendley provided an update on the huge operation to support the Fire Service 
while they were attending the recent fires at Holme Fen.  In answer to a request for 
emergency assistance from HDC the Mayor and Town Clerk had organised for food supplies 
to be provided to the firemen alongside that already organised by the Admiral Wells in Holme 
and Cllr Fendley had set up a Go Fund Me page for donations. There had been an amazing 
response from the community, with volunteers and local businesses providing food over the 
weekend and following days.  Cllr Fendley reported that the firemen had been overwhelmed 
by the response and hard work of all concerned and they would be issuing formal letters of 
thanks. There would be a further update on the Go Fund Me funds at the next meeting of the 
Town Council.  The Chief Fire Officer had been invited to attend the Mayor’s Civic Service in 
September. 
 
296. Meeting Dates 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council would take place on Thursday 10th September 
at 7pm.

held at 7pm on Thursday 13 August 2026 at  
Ramsey Town Council Great Whyte, Ramsey 
 
 
Present:  Councillors: I Axelsen, J Clarke, M Clarke, S Corney (Dep Mayor), A Costello, V 
Fendley (Mayor), L Knight, C Maskell, R Terrill, L Webster, and E Welsh. 
In attendance: Mrs L Renfree, Town Clerk  
274. Apologies for Absence. 
Cllrs J Aubin, A Austin, J Bufton, S Fice, and P Rose.

There were 10 members of the public present. 
 
277. Minutes of the Last Meeting to be Approved. 
To approve as a correct record, the minutes of the meeting Council held on 23rd July 2026, 
previously circulated. Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by Cllr R Terrill Ramsey Town 
Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to accept the minutes of 23rd July as a true record. 
 
278. Co-option of New Town Councillor. 
Three  candidates  put  themselves  forward  for  co-option,  each  applicant  addressed  the 
members giving an overview of themselves and why they felt they would be a good addition 
to the Town Council. The members voted and Jessie Thompson received the most votes and 
would join the council at their August planning meeting. 
 
279. District and County Councillor Update: 
Cllrs Coogan, Maheshwari and Tobias were invited to update members of District and County 
Council matters, apologies received from Cllr R Coogan, and a report tabled to members. No 
apologies from Cllr Maheshwari. Cllr Tobias reported back in person at the meeting as follows: 
Cllr  Tobias  informed members  that  he  does  not  use  social  media  to  conduct  his  council 
business  both  at  District  and  County  level  and is  looking  to  work in collaboration with  the 
council and residents, listening and challenging to make the Ramsey ward a better place to 
be. Since the Huntingdonshire District Council meeting Cllr Tobias had been looking into the 
parking assessment and challenging the fact there is no business case for spending £370,000 
of taxpayer’s money.  Cllr  Tobias  informed  members  that  some  Ramsey  plans  were  being 
discussed at the next Development Management Committee meeting. Cllr Tobias was happy 
to  support  CIL (Community  Infrastructure  Levy)  applications  if  they  will  support  the  wider 
community. From a County Council perspective Cllr Tobias had been in the role for 28 days 
and  had  planned  to  meet Highways  looking  at  the  road  infrastructure  and  is  looking  at  the 
Student Bus situation where the decision was made by the Peterborough College. The Clerk 
was asked to communicate with Cllr Tobias to continue the work asked of Cllr Maheshwari on 
securing the land for the car park on Mews Close. 
 
280. Planning Applications for Consideration 
1.1 26/01128/LBC – Injection of a SecoMUR chemical damp proof course into drilled holes to 
all external walls and solid brick internal walls- Bridge Farm 15 Ramsey Road, Ramsey Forty 
Foot. Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by Cllr M Clarke Ramsey Town Council voted 
UNANIMOUSLY for Huntingdonshire District Council to APPROVE the application. 
1.2  26/01328/HHFUL – Replacement  of  damaged  cladding to  front,  side  and  rear  of  the 
property- 17 Wyatt Close, Ramsey. Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by L Webster 
Ramsey   Town   Council   voted UNANIMOUSLY for   Huntingdonshire   District   Council   to 

2 
 
APPROVE the  application,  there  was  neighbouring  support  for  the application, and  it  is  in 
keeping with the area. 
1.3 26/01385/FUL- Change of use of land from agricultural to residential curtilage associated 
with Kingfisher House – Kingfisher House, Whittlesey Road, Benwick, March. Proposed by 
Cllr C Maskell and seconded by Cllr J Clarke Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY 
for Huntingdonshire District Council to APPROVE the application. 
1.4 26/01352/FUL – Change of use of land to a gypsy and traveller residential pitch 
comprising the siting of one mobile home, one amenity building, associated hardstanding 
and ancillary works (part retrospective). – Land East of Fern Cottage, Harpers Drove, 
Ramsey Heights. The Clerk had received objections to the application from residents of 
Ramsey Heights as previously agreed with Huntingdonshire District Council. The Clerk 
was asked to submit to the planning portal their objections as laid out in the 21-page 
report previously circulated. Cllr A Costello proposed REFUSAL and Cllr seconded by 
Cllr L Webster Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for the District Council to 
REFUSE this application. The Clerk would also put the residents comments to the 
planning portal. 
 
281. Planning Other Business: 
a) Pedestrianisation update: Cllr V Fendley informed members that the TRO was live and 
that there would be a planning application being submitted for the shop in a box units. 
b) Abbey College LHI BID- The plans were out for consultation and Ramsey Town 
Council were asked if they wanted to add any further comments on the plan. Ramsey 
Town Council did not want to add any further comments. 
c) Consultation on the Reviewed Bury Village Draft Neighbourhood Plan – Cllr V Fendley 
talked through the Goals and Objectives from the Bury Village Neighbourhood Plan 
and informed members it would be on the agenda for the next planning meeting for 
comment. 
d) To note the Tree Preservation Order26/002 – Ramsey Rural Museum had been 
confirmed. Noted 
e) Notice of application for a Town/ Village Green, Abbey Green, Ramsey. Noted. 
f) Huntingdonshire District Council Local Plan Consultation – Members to agree to using 
Anthony Northcote for advice regarding Ramsey Town Council’s response. Proposed 
by Cllr L Knight and seconded by Cllr R Terrill Ramsey town Council voted 10 FOR and 
1 AGAINST for the Clerk to instruct Anthony Northcote to give advice to Ramsey Town 
Council to comment on Huntingdonshire District Council’s Local Plan. 
282. Finance Items: 
a) Financial Summary – Cash book to 31/07/2026 tabled – Noted 
b) Expenditure Transactions to be approved – tabled- Proposed by Cllr S Corney and 
seconded by Cllr L Knight Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to agree the 
expenditure transactions. 
283. Working Part Recommendations: 
 Recommendations from the Economic Development Working Party 
a) For Ramsey Town Council to agree in principle to take control of the shop in a box 
units moving forward post successful TRO and Full Planning approval, and for 
Ramsey Town Council to manage the gated timings – Proposed by Cllr L Knight and 
seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council voted 10 FOR and 1 ABSTENTION 
for Ramsey Town Council to in principle take control of the Shop in a box units subject 
to a successful TRO and Full Planning approval. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and 

3 
 
seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council voted 10 FOR and 1 ABSTENTION 
for Ramsey Town Council to manage the gated timings. 
b) For Ramsey Town Council to initiate a Local Business Group to engage with our local 
businesses, with a view to sharing information. It was felt that a communication 
streamline to all Ramsey Parish Businesses was lacking and that this meeting would 
bring them together to explore a process moving forward. Proposed by Cllr L Knight 
and seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for a 
business meeting to be arranged in September. 
Recommendations from the Amenities, Highways, Health, and Leisure Working 
Party. 
a) For Ramsey Town Council to decide between two quotes for the Public Toilet Doors 
both quotes ex vat. The quote covers three new doors: Healthmatic £8040 or LAM 
Automation Ltd £8660 – The Clerk made an amendment to the cost of the 
Healthmatic quote £10,050. Proposed by Cllr A Costello and seconded by Cllr C 
Maskell Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to accept the quote from LAM 
Automation LTD at a cost of £8,660.00 and the funds would come from the CIL 
account.  
b) For Ramsey Town Council to decide if they want the public toilet doors to have 
windows in them at a cost of £700 ex vat. Proposed by Cllr J Clarke and seconded by 
Cllr C Maskell to REFUSE the windows in the public toilet doors. Ramsey Town 
Council voted REFUSE 6 and 3 AGAINST 2 ABSTENTIONS for the public toilets to 
not have windows. 
c) For Ramsey Town Council to agree in principle a large mural sited at the QEII 
Skatepark. Final design to be voted on in the future. - paper circulated. After a long 
discussion on the subject, it was agreed UNANIMOUSLY for the proposal to go back 
to Amenities, Highways, Health & Leisure for further exploration. 
Recommendations from the Communications Working Party. 
      a) To Agree the draft Digital Screen Policy for Ramsey Town Council previously                                                                                       
circulated. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council 
voted 10 FOR and 1 ABSTENTION to APPROVE the Digital Screen Policy. 
a) To Agree the Risk Assessment for Public Meetings at Ramsey Town Council- 
previously circulated. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and seconded by Cllr S 
Corney. Ramsey Town Council voted 9 FOR and 2 ABSTENTIONS to 
APPROVE the Risk Assessment for Public Meetings. 
b) To Agree the Risk Assessment for Premises and Buildings- previously 
circulated. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey 
Town Council vote 9 FOR and 2 ABSTENTIONS to APPROVE the Risk 
Assessment for Premises and Buildings. 
c) To Review the current IT Policy – previously circulated. Proposed by Cllr L 
Knight and seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council voted 10 FOR 
and 1 ABSTENTION to APPROVE the updated IT Policy. 
d) To agree the new email footer –tabled. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and 
seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council vote 10 FOR and 1 
ABSTENTION to use the footer tabled for Councillor emails. The Clerk will 
circulate to members to use. 
284. WORKING PARTY UPDATE  
a) Members to receive an update from the Chair of each Working Party- 
previously circulated. Cllr L Knight said this was a very useful document and is 
a really good idea. The document was noted. 
 
285. FEEDBACK FROM GRANT FROM COMMUNITY SAFETY & 
SAFETY PARTNERSHIP. 

4 
 
a) Feedback from Future Scooter Foundation -the Clerk showed two small video 
clips from some of the young people who participated in the evening event. 
There was a positive debate, and it was agreed that it would be good to have 
more young girls participating. Noted 
 
286. TOWN MAYOR’S AND CLERK’S CORRESPONDENCE: 
a) Update on Anti-Social Behaviour on the Clerk and Council. The Clerk updated 
members on the investigation with Huntingdonshire District Council Anti-Social 
behaviour team. They are now looking to produce a Criminal Behaviour Order 
to protect the Council. 
b) Resident communication on noise from skate park and concerns RTC would 
put lighting there for after dark use. The Clerk informed members that a 
resident after reading a District Councillors post on having lighting at the 
Skatepark was very upset as Ramsey Town Council had said that would not 
be the case. Cllr Fendley was very clear that there would be no plans to light 
up the Skatepark. 
c) Resident communication on thanking the Town Council for the work Paul and 
Morgan are doing keeping the Cemetery clear and improving the area. The 
Clerk informed members that positive comments had been received about the 
work in clearing the Cemetery. 
d) Thank you from the Ramsey Garden and Horticulture Club for the grant we 
gave them which enable two new competitions this year. Cllr Fendley informed 
members of the letter received thanking Ramsey Town Council for their grant 
and the opportunities it has given their club. 
e) Ramsey Heights residents concern over lack of Fire Hydrant for the Droves. 
After the fire on Harpers Drove, residents were concerned that the Fire Service 
had to keep going away to refill the tanker. This was noted. 
Councillor Costello left the meeting at 8:55pm. 
287. ATTENDANCES AT MEETINGS AND ORGANISATIONS: 
a) Safer Communities Public Meeting - Cllr V Fendley fed back on the public 
meeting held at Ramsey Forty Foot. Cllr V Fendley praised the Inspector for 
his honesty during the meeting, but the overall outcome was we do live in a 
safe community. 
b) Mayor met with County Councillor Cllr H Tobias. Cllr V Fendley informed 
members that she had had a meeting and discussed the LHI bids and 
infrastructure. 
c) Magnolia Park Opening Day- Cllr V Fendley attended the opening and it was a 
very positive day. 
d) Jones Court 40
th
 Anniversary BBQ – Cllr V Fendley and the Clerk attended the 
BBQ, and Cllr V Fendley had the difficult task of judging the baking 
competition. 
e) Update on correspondence with Cambridgeshire Constabulary – Cllr R Terrill 
updated members on his conversation with Inspector Norden. 
f) MP Sam Carling – Local Surgery Date 14
th
 August 2026. Cllr V Fendley 
informed members that the MP was in the community meeting with residents. 
 
288. MEETING DATES 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council (Planning) will take place on 27th August 
2026 at 7pm.
